title: StrongARM latch comparator
topology: A dynamic, clocked regenerative comparator. During the reset (clock-low) phase, clocked PMOS pull-up devices reset both internal drain nodes to VDD while a tail switch holds the input differential pair off. When the clock goes high, the tail current source turns on and the input pair's differential currents discharge the two internal drain nodes at rates set by the differential input; once the two nodes diverge enough, a cross-coupled NMOS/PMOS latch pair (a back-to-back inverter pair) regenerates that small initial imbalance into a full-rail digital output at very high speed. Because it only conducts current during the brief clocked evaluation/regeneration transient, the comparator draws essentially zero static bias current between clock edges.
spec_class: high-speed, zero-static-power clocked comparator core for SAR ADC quantizers, clock-and-data-recovery samplers, and other PHY-class decision circuits needing sub-nanosecond regeneration with no continuous bias current

pdk_portability.notes: The clocked-regenerative-latch topology and its offset/kickback trade-offs are fully portable to any bulk CMOS PDK with complementary devices; the achievable regeneration speed (set by the cross-coupled inverter pair's transconductance and the internal node capacitances) and the input-pair-referred offset from device mismatch are sky130-specific, since they depend on sky130's minimum-length intrinsic gain and threshold-mismatch (AVt) characteristics, which are worse than a scaled finFET node and typically call for larger-than-minimum input-pair devices to reach sub-millivolt offset targets without added calibration.

sizing_approach: Size the input differential pair's transconductance and channel length for the required input-referred offset (a larger device area, or longer length, reduces threshold-mismatch-driven offset per Pelgrom-style area scaling, at the cost of added input capacitance and stronger kickback); size the tail current/reset switch for the desired regeneration start time relative to the clock edge; size the cross-coupled latch pair for fast regeneration by keeping its node capacitance low and its devices' transconductance high relative to that capacitance, since the regeneration time constant scales with node capacitance divided by latch transconductance; size the reset PMOS pull-up transistors so the reset time is much shorter than the available clock low-phase, ensuring the comparator fully re-arms every cycle; when offset must be reduced further without growing the input pair indefinitely, add a systematic offset-cancellation technique (e.g. capacitive trimming or switched calibration at the input or at the latch cross-coupling nodes) rather than continuing to scale device area.
layout_idioms: input differential pair laid out common-centroid, matched to the same discipline as an OTA input pair, since StrongARM offset is dominated by input-pair threshold-voltage mismatch

cross-coupled latch inverter pair laid out with mirror symmetry about the differential output nodes to avoid a systematic, layout-induced offset that a randomly mismatched pair alone would not exhibit

clock (reset) switch transistors placed symmetrically on both half-circuits with matched clock routing length and loading, to avoid differential clock-induced charge injection between the two internal output nodes
minimum practical, symmetric routing on the two internal drain nodes to minimize kickback-noise asymmetry coupled back onto the input pair and the driving reference or signal source

source.citation: B. Razavi, "The StrongARM Latch [A Circuit for All Seasons]," IEEE Solid-State Circuits Magazine, vol. 7, no. 2, pp. 12-17, Spring 2015.
source.license_or_openness: Peer-reviewed IEEE magazine article cited here for its topology description, offset/kickback analysis, and design considerations only (no figures or text reproduced), per the KB's open-sources sourcing rule (case 2, peer-reviewed paywalled literature cited for restated methodology only, in kb/SOURCING.md). This article is the standard modern reference for the topology and its history, tracing it to its original use in the DEC Alpha 21164 microprocessor's clock receiver.

notes: Named after its origin in the DEC/Digital StrongARM and Alpha microprocessor clock-receiver circuits (via J. Montanaro et al., 'A 160-MHz, 32-b, 0.5-W CMOS RISC Microprocessor,' IEEE JSSC, vol. 31, no. 11, Nov. 1996, which this entry does not separately cite in detail but which the Razavi article above traces the topology to). The zero-static-current property makes it attractive versus a continuously-biased comparator (e.g. the five-transistor OTA used open-loop) whenever the application is inherently clocked, at the cost of comparatively higher offset and kickback than a statically-biased, offset-calibrated design.
